units.title: Construct: Owning handles and the partial-initialization frontier
steps: Derive the construction frontier invariant and distinguish acquired storage, initialized object state and published ownership; compare explicit C cleanup with automatic language destruction.
Implement transactional three-resource construction and idempotent destruction using the accepted typed allocator callback ABI, proving which prefix is owned at each failure point.

Three successful takes publish count3; two destroy calls together perform exactly three releases. A zero middle count causes no allocator invocation.

Inject failure on each acquisition, reject zero and overflowing lengths before any callback, instrument release order and exactly-once counts, and test repeated destruction. Kill the omitted-rollback mutant. Extend the anchor with a callback trace that proves reverse order, not just equal release totals.
reasoning: Derive the construction frontier invariant and distinguish acquired storage, initialized object state and published ownership; compare explicit C cleanup with automatic language destruction.
deliverables: Implement transactional three-resource construction and idempotent destruction using the accepted typed allocator callback ABI, proving which prefix is owned at each failure point.

Inject failure on each acquisition, reject zero and overflowing lengths before any callback, instrument release order and exactly-once counts, and test repeated destruction. Kill the omitted-rollback mutant. Extend the anchor with a callback trace that proves reverse order, not just equal release totals.

Replace the prefix with a dependency graph: acquire A, then B and C independently, then D requiring B. Write an initialized-set representation and reverse dependency cleanup. Delayed assessment makes C initialization fail after its storage acquisition; distinguish storage release from destruction of a constructed value.

units.title: Construct: Scoped cleanup, conditional undo and publication by swap
steps: Explain when a cleanup stack is a resource protocol, when an undo log is a semantic rollback protocol, and why neither automatically reverses already published external effects.

Enumerate all success/failure policy combinations through depth4 against an independent reversed-list filter, test capacity8/9 and callback reentrancy rejection, inject failure before every registration, and trace publication before old cleanup. Kill a mutant that executes every conditional cleanup.
reasoning: Explain when a cleanup stack is a resource protocol, when an undo log is a semantic rollback protocol, and why neither automatically reverses already published external effects.
deliverables: Implement conditional LIFO cleanup and publication-by-swap with explicit callback effects, stack capacity, transferred ownership and nonlocal-exit restrictions.

units.title: Construct: Move protocols, source poisoning and the limits of must-use diagnostics
steps: Separate ownership transfer, physical byte copying, source poisoning and diagnostic enforcement; explain why ISO C17 cannot prevent all implicit copies of this public struct.
Implement checked move/consume operations and an isolated diagnostic probe that intentionally ignores OW_MUST_USE, with extension-enabled and portable builds reported separately.
checks: After moving three blocks, destination.count=3 and source.count=0. Consuming the source returns DEAD; consuming the destination releases three blocks once; a second consume returns DEAD. A direct C assignment copying the original owner is a counterexample to an alleged static move-only guarantee.

Test self-move, occupied destination, empty source, repeated consumption and allocator release counts. Reject the source-not-poisoned mutant. Compile a copied owner without consuming both copies: use it as a static counterexample, not an unbounded double-free experiment. Record whether GCC/Clang actually emit the ignored-result diagnostic.
reasoning: Separate ownership transfer, physical byte copying, source poisoning and diagnostic enforcement; explain why ISO C17 cannot prevent all implicit copies of this public struct.

units.title: Construct: Runtime borrow tracking, range splitting and finite token identities
steps: Derive reader/writer interval exclusion separately from pointer lifetime, then explain finite identity exhaustion and why a runtime token does not prevent illicit raw aliases.
Implement bounded acquire/release and transactional writer splitting with arithmetic-safe extent checks, generation retirement and an explicit guard ownership rule.
checks: A writer[0,8) blocks a reader[3,4). Splitting it at3 creates[0,3) and[3,8), invalidates the parent token and admits no gap or overlap. A writer[8,8) may coexist because it touches no element. A released token cannot release a later loan in the same slot.

Use an independent finite-set intersection oracle for all small extents/ranges/read-write combinations, then test SIZE_MAX bounds and UINT32_MAX serial retirement. Exhaust the slot table before split and compare complete pre/post books and output canaries. Kill the conflict-check omission mutant; explain that reduced exhaustive checks do not prove arbitrary C lifetimes.
reasoning: Derive reader/writer interval exclusion separately from pointer lifetime, then explain finite identity exhaustion and why a runtime token does not prevent illicit raw aliases.
deliverables: Implement bounded acquire/release and transactional writer splitting with arithmetic-safe extent checks, generation retirement and an explicit guard ownership rule.

Use an independent finite-set intersection oracle for all small extents/ranges/read-write combinations, then test SIZE_MAX bounds and UINT32_MAX serial retirement. Exhaust the slot table before split and compare complete pre/post books and output canaries. Change numeric intervals into a strided view: two disjoint bounding intervals are sufficient but not necessary for disjoint element sets. Delayed assessment splits a two-dimensional tile with padding; derive exact touched indices and decide whether a conservative rejection or richer borrow representation is justified.

units.title: Construct: Strong and weak ownership with atomic and non-atomic counts
steps: Prove the distinct value/control lifetimes, no-resurrection property and count-overflow behavior; distinguish reference-count synchronization from pointee synchronization and cycle collection.

Implement strong/weak ownership twice, first under exclusion and then with C17 atomics, documenting initialization publication, owned-reference preconditions, callback effects and each memory-order edge.
checks: Downgrade, retain, drop, drop yields strong0,weak1, one value destruction and no control reclamation. Upgrade now fails DEAD. Dropping the remaining weak reclaims the control once. Four threads each retain/drop5000 times while holding their own strong reference; after all owned strong references end, destruction occurs once, and a retained weak keeps the control available for a failed upgrade.

Trace every strong/weak boundary with an independent counter model, test maximum-count refusal, and reject omission of the implicit weak release. Run the actual four-thread anchor, separate TSan if available, GCC/Clang optimized and ASan/UBSan builds, inspect atomic lowering and report lock-free status. A quiet race detector does not prove the memory-order argument or reclaim safety for fabricated references.
reasoning: Prove the distinct value/control lifetimes, no-resurrection property and count-overflow behavior; distinguish reference-count synchronization from pointee synchronization and cycle collection.
deliverables: Implement strong/weak ownership twice, first under exclusion and then with C17 atomics, documenting initialization publication, owned-reference preconditions, callback effects and each memory-order edge.
